title: Rapture and return
hook: some Protestants expect believers to be caught up before tribulation; other Christians read 1 Thessalonians 4 differently

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bible's near-last words, and an old Aramaic one: maranatha. Your line was come, Lord Jesus.

A bumper sticker warns that the car may suddenly be driverless. Novels and films show people vanishing mid-sentence, clothes left in a heap on the seat. Some Christians call that coming moment the rapture; other Christians grew up in churches where it was never taught. It came up briefly back on day two hundred sixteen, on the Mount of Olives. Both groups read the same short passage, a few lines near the end of Paul's first letter to the church in Thessalonica.

First, why Paul wrote it. Not to give a timetable. Some in the young church had died, and the living were grieving and afraid: "I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope." It begins as a letter to people at a graveside. Second, the picture: "For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air." The word rapture isn't in the King James text. It says caught up. Third, the readings. Some Protestants, many of them dispensationalists, read a gathering of believers before a time of great tribulation, with Christ's visible return later. Other Christians, among them the Catholic and Orthodox churches and other Protestants, read it as part of Christ's one return at the end: the dead raised, the living gathered up to meet him. Some readers hear in meet a town going out to greet an arriving guest and walk him back in: a welcome party. Fourth, the lines Paul ends on: "and so shall we ever be with the Lord. Wherefore comfort one another with these words." Whatever the timetable, Paul ends with together, and with comfort.

Read 1 Thessalonians four, verses thirteen to eighteen, slowly, out loud if you can, and let one phrase stay: "comfort one another with these words." Bring to mind someone who is grieving, or someone you've lost; there's no question about the end to settle, only the people the letter was written for. If you pray, hold them before God; if not, hold them in mind. And if grief feels too heavy to carry alone, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Rapture. A name, not in the King James text, for being caught up to meet the Lord in the air. Christians read the passage in more than one way.
Your line: ever with the Lord. From all things new to come, Lord Jesus, this week ended in comfort. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Protestant churches teach a rapture of believers before a time of tribulation; the Catholic and Orthodox churches and other Protestants read 1 Thessalonians 4 as part of Christ's one return, and some churches read the passage at funerals.

chat.who: a friend who grew up in church
chat.says: My church never taught the rapture. Did we miss something everyone believes?
options: Churches differ: some read Paul as a gathering before a tribulation, others as part of Christ's one return.
Yes, every church has always taught it the same way, so your church simply left it out by mistake.
No, the idea comes only from Revelation; Paul never wrote a word about being caught up.
